paras: Every year, legislative committees invite hundreds of experts to testify about reports they have spent months or years writing. Most of these witnesses know their subject better than anyone in the room. And yet many of them leave the session feeling that it went badly. The problem is rarely the content. It is the format: three minutes to open, and then questions from people who are not always looking for the truth.

Experienced witnesses prepare the three minutes differently. They do not try to cover the whole report. They condense it into three or four events, usually expressed as nouns: the adoption of a model, the renegotiation of a contract, the rise in investment. And they attach a source to every number, because the first question from a skeptical member is almost always the same: where does that number come from?

The questions are where most witnesses lose control. Some are fair, and some are loaded: they contain a hidden idea, so that a simple yes or no makes the witness look bad. The veterans do not accept the hidden idea. They name it calmly, and then they answer the real issue. They also never guess a number. If they do not know it, they say so, and promise to send it in writing.

Finally, they correct themselves quickly. A witness who says a wrong figure and repairs it in one sentence looks more rigorous, not less. Committees forgive mistakes. What they do not forgive is a witness who seems to be hiding something.
reading.source: A composite of advice given to expert witnesses before legislative committees, written for this lesson.

listenings.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to this session of the infrastructure committee. Before we hear from our witnesses, a few rules. Each witness has three minutes for an opening statement. Three minutes, not four. If you go over, I will stop you, politely but firmly, and your full written statement will still be part of the record. After the statements, each member of the committee has five minutes for questions. Members, please ask questions, not speeches. And one request to our witnesses: for every number you give us today, please tell us where it comes from. This committee has heard many numbers over the years, and not all of them were real. Our first witness is an expert on port concessions. You have three minutes.

I have testified before committees about forty times, and I have three rules. The first is about numbers. Never guess. If a member asks you for a number and you do not know it, say: I do not have the exact figure, and I will send it to the committee in writing. Nobody has ever lost credibility by saying that. Many people have lost it by guessing. The second rule is about mistakes. You will make one. When you do, correct it immediately, in one sentence, and continue. A quick correction makes you look more careful, not less. The third rule is about loaded questions, the ones like: so you admit that the policy failed? Do not say yes, and do not say no. Name the assumption, calmly: that question assumes the policy failed. Then answer the real issue. It works almost every time.
